'''Tirahi''' is a nearly extinct if not already extinct<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ethnologue.com/language/tra|title=Tirahi|website=Ethnologue|access-date=2016-04-27|quote=It is very likely that this language is extinct. The Tirahi are “a group of unclear origin, almost completely assimilated by Pashtun” (Pstrusinska and Gray 1990).}}</ref> [[Indo-Aryan languages|Indo-Aryan language]]<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9WroLC__7EUC|title=Encyclopaedia of the Linguistic Sciences: Issues and Theories|last=Prakāśaṃ|first=Vennelakaṇṭi|date=2008-01-01|publisher=Allied Publishers|isbn=9788184242799|page=143|language=en}}</ref> spoken in a few villages in the southeast of [[Jalalabad]] in the [[Nangarhar Province]] of eastern [[Afghanistan]].  It is spoken by older adults, who are likewise fluent in [[Pashto]].<ref name=e15/>

The [[Tirahis]] were expelled from [[Tirah]] in the present-day [[Khyber District]] of [[Khyber Pakhtunkhwa]], Pakistan, by the [[Afridi]] Pashtuns.<ref>{{cite book |last=Konow |first=Sten |author-link=Sten Konow |date=1933 |title=Acta Orientalia, Volumes 11-12 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mg1KAAAAYAA |publisher=Munksgaard |page=161}}</ref> [[Georg Morgenstierne]] claimed that Tirahi is "probably the remnant of a dialect group extending from Tirah through the [[Peshawar District|Peshawar district]] into [[Swat District|Swat]] and [[Dir (region)|Dir]]."<ref name="morg"/>

== Geographic distribution ==
Spoken in the [[Nangarhar Province]] of Northeastern Afghanistan, there are about 100 native speakers today, if any. This is mainly due to the majority of the [[Tirahi|Tirahi people]] having assimilated into the dominant [[Pashtuns|Pashtun]] culture. Tirahi is also spoken in a couple of villages southeast of the Afghan city of [[Jalalabad]],<ref name="ReferenceA">{{cite journal|last1=Voegelin|first1=C.F.|last2=Voegelin|first2=F.M.|title=Languages of the World: Indo-European Fascicle One|journal=Anthropological Linguistics|date=1965|volume=7|page=286}}</ref> such as Jaba, Mitarani, and Bara-khel.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Stein|first1=Aurel|title=Notes on Tirahi. The Speakers of Tirahi|journal=The Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society of Great Britain and Ireland|date=Jul 1925|volume=3|pages=401–402}}</ref>

== Classification ==
Tirahi is an [[Indo-Aryan languages|Indo-Aryan language]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Grierson|first=George|date=March 1925|title=On The Tirahi Language|jstor=25220761|journal=The Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society of Great Britain and Ireland|issue=3|page=408}}</ref> Further, Tirahi is part of the sub-group of [[Dardic languages|Kohistani languages]] along with languages such as [[Bateri language|Bateri]], [[Chilisso language|Chilisso]], [[Gowro language|Gowro]], and others. However, Tirahi also shares with languages spoken further to the east, such as [[Kashmiri language|Kashmiri]].<ref name=":0" /> As a Dardic Language, Tirahi strongly preserves some vocabulary of spoken Sanskrit (cow - dēn in Tirahi,  dhēnuh in Sanskrit, hand - ast in Tirahi, hastah in Sanskrit).<ref name=":0" /> Being a language spoken in Afghanistan, Tirahi shares various words and grammatical constructs with [[Pashto]], a language spoken throughout Afghanistan to which many Tirahi speakers have become accustomed to speaking. Since Tirahi is entirely separated from the other Dardic languages, located south of the [[Kabul River]] and west of the [[Khyber Pass]], rendering it wholly encased by Pashto.<ref name="ReferenceA"/> Tirahi also shares some vocabulary with [[Kashmiri language|Kashmiri]] and [[Shina language|Shina]] such as the Tirahi ''mala'', for a father, the Kashmiri ''mol'', and the Shina ''malo''.<ref name="Grierson, G. 1925">Grierson, G. (1925). On the Tirahi language. Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society (New Series), 57(03), 405-416.</ref>

== Grammar ==

Tirahi shows much influence from [[Pashto]] in phonology, lexicon and even morphology. However, its vocabulary exhibits a connection to Kohistani dialects. Therefore, Tirahi seems to occupy an intermediate position between [[Pashto]] and the [[Kohistani people|Kohistani]] group.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=C9MPCd6mO6sC|title=The Indo-Aryan Languages|last1=Jain|first1=Dhanesh|last2=Cardona|first2=George|date=2003-01-01|publisher=Routledge|isbn=9780700711307|page=857|language=en}}</ref> Morgenstirne claims that Tirahi is "probably the remnant of a dialect group extending from Tirahi through the [[Peshawar District|Peshawar district]] into [[Swat District|Swat]] and [[Dir (region)|Dir]]."<ref name="morg">{{Cite journal|last=Turner|first=R. L.|date=1934-01-01|title=Review of Report on a Linguistic Mission to North-Western India|jstor=25201006|journal=Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society of Great Britain and Ireland|issue=4|pages=801–803| volume=66|  doi=10.1017/S0035869X00112675}}</ref>

=== Nouns and adjectives ===

Tirahi is an [[Inflection|inflected]] language, having 5 cases: [[Nominative]], Oblique, [[Genitive case|Genitive]], [[Dative case|Dative]], and [[Ablative case|Ablative]]. Adjectives, verbs, and nouns usually agree according to gender. Consonant-final nouns add e or an along with their traditional endings.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=C9MPCd6mO6sC|title=The Indo-Aryan Languages|last1=Jain|first1=Dhanesh|last2=Cardona|first2=George|date=2003-01-01|publisher=Routledge|isbn=9780700711307|pages=857–9, also for all grammatical information below|language=en}}</ref> There appears to be an indefinite article, added to the end of the word as an -ī, similar to [[Farsi]].<ref name=":0" />

==== Verbs ====
# Non finite forms
## Infinitive: stem + an (''karan -'' 'to do/make') 
# Tense-aspect forms
## Imperative Singular: stem, Imperative Plural: stem + V 
## Present-future: root + endings -  1st: - m, 2nd: -s, 3rd: -e, 1st plural: -en
## Definite Present: da/de + present-future

==== Example sentences ====
* ''Abo-e kata dur thi?''  ('Village' +  'how much far' +  'is')
** "How far is your village?"
* ''Pali de kham'' ('Bread' + Definite Future + 'Eat')
** "I am eating bread." 
* ''La brok odasta ga'' ('He' + 'Very' + 'Hungry' + 'become/go')
** "He became very hungry"
* ''Ao mara ga-m'' ('I' + 'die' + 'become') 
** "I died/am dead"
